title: International trends in water utility regimes
rationale: The retrieved full text matches the record metadata (Madhoo 2007, Annals of Public and Cooperative Economics). Most of the paper (Sections 1-3.3 and 4) is a non-systematic narrative taxonomy of public/private water utility regimes, residential and industrial water tariff structures, secondary literature on affordability, and agricultural irrigation water rights and pricing. Its sole original empirical component (Section 3.4) is a cross-country ordered logistic regression across 32 countries testing how nationwide utility ownership share, water availability, socioeconomic factors, and World Bank governance/transparency/stability indices affect national utility cost recovery (CostRec, scored 1-5 according to O&M and capital cost recovery). Because the empirical study measures only utility/sector financial cost recovery rather than household or community water/sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (and also relies on macro-level ownership share and macro-governance indices rather than a rule-type mechanism governing service access), the study is excluded as E04 (Wrong outcome). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the decision remains exclude due to the lack of an eligible empirical access or affordability outcome.

title: Water, sanitation and hygiene: measuring gender equality and empowerment
rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). This 3-page 'Perspectives' article in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization (Kayser et al., 2019) is a narrative commentary critiquing current WASH gender-equality and empowerment monitoring indicators across four priority areas and proposing future research directions. It presents no primary empirical data, no empirical methodology and no systematic review synthesis, and it also does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative or regulatory mechanism governing WASH service access under Criterion 2.

title: Environmental survey of segregated habitats of Roma in Hungary: a way to be empowering and reliable in minority research
rationale: This empirical nationwide environmental survey maps 758 segregated Roma colonies across 19 Hungarian counties and reports colony-level lack of piped water mains and lack of sewerage/drainage (satisfying C1, C3, C4, and C6). It does not examine any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor—under either the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope or the plain wording of Criterion 2—as an exposure governing water or sanitation service access. Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure).

rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). title: Slum upgrading strategies involving physical environment and infrastructure interventions and their effects on health and socio-economic outcomes
rationale: This Cochrane systematic review (Turley et al., 2013) synthesizes 5 main studies (1 cluster-RCT, 4 cluster-CBAs) and 9 supporting studies (6 CPIs, 3 UBAs) evaluating in situ slum upgrading programmes involving physical environment and infrastructure improvements in LMIC urban slums. Although the review primarily focuses on health and general socio-economic outcomes, it explicitly prespecifies and reports water-affordability outcomes (monthly water expenditure and share of household income spent on water in Galiani 2007 and Aiga 2002) as well as process/fidelity and qualitative findings on water/sanitation connection coverage and fee-related public tap shutoffs, satisfying c1, c3, and c4. However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): the required intervention is generic physical infrastructure project delivery (installing water connections, latrines, drains, road paving, or cement floors vs. no intervention), optional legal/tenure co-components in multicomponent upgrading packages are not isolated or evaluated as rules governing water/sanitation access, and institutional/governance contexts remain unanalysed background. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because municipal, privatised, and community-managed upgrading delivery arrangements and bundled tenure packages constitute broad institutional/governance interventions.

title: Provision of basic services in slums: A review of the evidence on top-down and bottom-up approaches
rationale: Devkar et al. (2019) is a full-text English systematic empirical synthesis of 104 primary studies (77 water, 64 sanitation, 31 electricity; 568 coded evidence items) examining basic service access in urban slums across developing countries. Inclusion Criterion 3 explicitly encompasses systematic empirical syntheses. While its overarching numerical categorization compares top-down (government/public utility) versus bottom-up (NGO/CBO/private small-scale provider) approaches, its line-by-line thematic synthesis and core findings directly analyze rule-type legal, administrative, and regulatory mechanisms governing water and sanitation access—including legal recognition/notification status of slums, tenure and house-ownership documentation barriers, institutional guarantor accommodations, statutory utility mandates to expand networks into informal areas, creation of a pro-poor WSS regulator, private-concession regulatory gaps, municipal demolition enforcement, and connection-fee/tariff rules—satisfying both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 alongside Criteria 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6.
